claims.text: Conventional preparation of single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 is prone to porosity and associated service weakness.
SPS can densify single-phase ZrB2 at approximately 1900–2100 °C.
SPS provides rapid processing or consolidation compared with conventional processing.
Rapid heating and transient high local temperatures during SPS enhance ZrB2 densification and reduce porosity.
Pulsed electrical current during SPS generates localized hotspots in ZrB2.
Pulsed electrical current and localized hotspots enhance diffusion in ZrB2.
Enhanced diffusion during SPS promotes grain-boundary healing.
SPS-induced consolidation and grain-boundary healing produce fewer processing-induced defects.
Reducing processing-induced defects makes ZrB2 less susceptible to hole formation during liquid plating-bath exposure.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have equivalent or improved mechanical strength relative to conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have significantly lower porosity than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit fewer holes during long-duration liquid plating-bath exposure.
The high temperature used in conventional ZrB2 preparation causes higher porosity and structural defects.
Porosity and structural defects in conventionally prepared ZrB2 cause premature failure under liquid plating conditions.
Optimal SPS parameters for ZrB2 have not been fully established.
Variations in SPS pulse conditions or sintering duration may produce unpredictable ZrB2 microstructures.
Scaling SPS from laboratory experiments to industrial processing may introduce additional uncertainty.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits mechanical strength equivalent to the conventional control, whereas the falsification rule requires a statistically significant improvement in mechanical strength; an equivalent-strength result could therefore satisfy the prediction but trigger falsification.
